questions.question: What is the core product invariant for inline completion?
options: Typing never waits for inference, and generated text enters the document only after explicit acceptance.
Every eligible keystroke must display a suggestion.
The server owns the draft while a request is active.
Late suggestions should be inserted once the user pauses.
questions.explanation: Completion is an optional proposal path. The editor and writer remain authoritative even when every suggestion dependency fails.

questions.question: Why should the client attach a draft and cursor version to each request?
options: To make stale responses safe to discard after the writer changes the document.
To let the model overwrite older user text.
To increase candidate count without extra latency.
To share personalized prefixes across accounts.
questions.explanation: A version binds a candidate to the exact editor state it observed. A mismatch means the response is stale, regardless of its score.

questions.question: A path spends 8 ms in the client, 16 ms on the network, 11 ms encoding context, 27 ms in inference, 12 ms decoding three candidates, and 7 ms on release checks. Does it fit an 82 ms deadline?
options: Yes, the path takes 81 ms and leaves 1 ms of headroom.
Yes, the path takes 70 ms and leaves 12 ms of headroom.
No, the path exceeds the deadline by 1 ms.
The result cannot be calculated without acceptance rate.
questions.explanation: The complete path is 8 + 16 + 11 + 27 + 12 + 7 = 81 ms. Model time is only one part of the interaction budget.

questions.question: Why can the highest-ranked candidate still be suppressed?
options: Ranking orders candidates, but hard gates such as safety, freshness, and draft identity remain independent.
The highest score always indicates repeated text.
Only the lowest-ranked candidate should be visible.
Suppression is required whenever more than one candidate was generated.
questions.explanation: A weighted score must not average away a failed invariant. Unsafe or stale text is rejected even when it is otherwise relevant.

questions.question: Which metric best complements acceptance rate when measuring whether suggestions save useful work?
options: Accepted characters that remain after later edits, sliced with undo and overwrite behavior.
Model parameter count.
Raw keydown event volume.
Average training batch size.
questions.explanation: Acceptance alone can reward trivial or quickly deleted text. Retained accepted characters and reversal behavior better connect the feature to user value.

questions.question: An experiment improves accepted characters overall but regresses one supported language slice. What should the rollout controller do?
options: Hold expansion and investigate the failing slice rather than hiding it inside the average.
Expand because the overall metric is positive.
Remove language from telemetry.
Raise traffic to make the slice smaller.
questions.explanation: Rollout gates should protect governed slices. Aggregate improvement does not compensate for a known harmful regression.

questions.question: What is the correct degraded behavior when the required safety policy service is unavailable?
options: Suppress suggestions and keep ordinary editing available.
Bypass the policy service to preserve coverage.
Block the editor until policy recovers.
Reuse a candidate from another account.
questions.explanation: A required release gate fails closed for generated text, while the primary editor remains fully usable.
